events.title: Cocks invents RSA at GCHQ
events.summary: Clifford Cocks invented a public-key encryption scheme equivalent to [RSA] at GCHQ in 1973 — years before the public [RSA] announcement.
events.about: Cocks' classified work remained secret until 1997 — revealing that British intelligence had discovered public-key cryptography independently. His story illustrates how security research often happened in parallel inside government labs.

narrative.whyChosen: Cocks' work proved public-key encryption was discoverable before the academic breakthrough.
narrative.whyImportant: It showed the ideas behind [RSA] were not a single-lab accident but a natural next step.
narrative.problemSolved: Secure government communications needed key distribution without exposing secrets.

events.title: Xerox Alto operational
events.summary: Xerox PARC's Alto workstation became operational in 1973 — the first computer designed around a bitmap [GUI], mouse, and [Ethernet] networking.
events.about: The Alto ran [Bravo] word processing and [Smalltalk] — Steve Jobs saw it and pushed the Macintosh toward [GUI] computing. [Ethernet], [WYSIWYG] editing, and overlapping windows were prototyped here years before they reached consumer [PC]s. Developers study Alto as the ancestor of every desktop and laptop UI.

narrative.whyChosen: The Alto was the first personal workstation built for graphical computing from the ground up.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved [GUI]s, networking, and laser printing belonged on every desk — not just lab demos.
narrative.problemSolved: Researchers needed an interactive machine for document preparation and [distributed computing], not batch punch cards.

events.title: Ethernet invented at Xerox PARC
events.summary: Robert Metcalfe and colleagues developed [Ethernet] at Xerox PARC in 1973 — a [packet switching] [LAN] for connecting Alto workstations.
events.about: Ethernet's CSMA/CD design let many machines share a coax cable cheaply — a pattern DEC, Intel, and Xerox standardized in 1980 and that still underlies wired office and datacenter networking today (now switched, not shared bus).

narrative.whyChosen: [Ethernet] became the dominant LAN technology for four decades.
narrative.whyImportant: It made networking [PC]s and workstations affordable before Wi-Fi existed.
narrative.problemSolved: Labs needed to link computers, printers, and file servers without point-to-point serial links.
